title: 400 HP Under $40K: 5 Cars and 1 Truck That Bring Bang for Buck

body_markdown:
Last month, the average price for a new automobile in the U.S. cracked[50 grand](https://www.freep.com/story/money/cars/2026/09/12/average-new-car-prices-soar-above-50000-for-the-first-time-this-year/91716076007/) for the first time. And that’s *average* stuff. Toyota Highlanders, Honda Passports, Lincoln Corsairs. That kind of thing. As always, though, one need only to start shopping vintage (aka used) to realize that you can get much more exciting stuff for less money. So, we went through our current price guide, set a theoretical money-saving budget of 40 grand, and saw which fast cars we could find. “Fast,” of course, is always relative, but in this case, a 400-horsepower engine and post-2000 build date seemed like a good barrier. Below are the best deals we came across.


## 2009 Pontiac G8 GXP


DW Burnett


**Engine: 376 cid/415 hp V-8**


**Condition #2 value:[$39,200](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/pontiac/g8/2009/2009-pontiac-g8-gxp?id=aCn1I000000DUTLSA4)**


Based on an Australian Holden platform like its two-door[GTO](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/pontiac/gto/2006/2006-pontiac-gto-base?id=aCn1I000000DUyMSAW) cousin, the G8 was the last full-size sedan to wear Pontiac’s red arrowhead. Base models came with a bland V-6, but stepping up to the GT model got you a 361-hp V-8, and the GXP model got you an LS3 rated at 415 ponies, driving the rear wheels and optional with a six-speed manual. It proved an unprofitable exercise through Pontiac’s demise in 2009.


In the grips of the Great Recession, a brand-new G8 GXP started at a little under 40 grand, and that’s about where these cars sit today, when they’re in excellent low-mile condition. After peaking at $40,400 in 2022, condition #2 values have now slid to $39,200. Which isn’t exactly cheap, and the Holden-based GM cars can have some surprising headaches in terms of parts, but the GXP is still one of the great sleeper sedans of the 2000s.


## 2012–13 Ford Mustang Boss 302


Mecum


**Engine: 302 cid/444 hp V-8**


**Condition #2 value:[$34,100](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/mustang/2012/2012-ford-mustang-boss_302?id=aCn1I000000CyQ9SAK)**


The original Boss 302 came out in[1969](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/mustang/1969/1969-ford-mustang-boss_302?id=aCn1I000000DWFXSA4) and was Ford’s answer to the[Z/28 Camaro](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/camaro/1968/1968-chevrolet-camaro-z!!28?id=aCn1I000000CzH2SAK) in Trans Am racing. Ford won the Trans Am title in 1970 and dropped the Boss 302 model for 1971. But, Ford being Ford, it was only a matter of time before it played the history and heritage card with a revived Boss 302 package, and that time came in 2012.


Providing the pony car with added muscle to back up the historic badge, Ford gave the 5.0-liter Coyote V-8 ported alloy heads and hotter cams with variable timing. Horsepower rose from 412 in the standard Mustang GT to 444 in the Boss. Meanwhile, a beefier suspension with adjustable shocks and struts, as well as bigger tires, allowed this special ‘Stang to rip 1.0 g of lateral acceleration.


The 2012 Boss 302 started at a little over $40K when it was new, and though it appears to be done doing used-car depreciation, it’s still attainable in the mid-$30K range, even for very good low-mile examples. There was also a “[Laguna Seca](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/mustang/2012/2012-ford-mustang-boss_302_laguna_seca?id=aCn1I000000DFaiSAG) ” edition of the Boss 302, named after the famous California road course. This model got additional upgrades like a limited-slip differential and revised suspension, but since Ford sold just 750 copies, they command a serious premium and cost about 10 grand more than a standard version.


## 2020–21 Chevrolet Camaro LT1


GM


**Engine: 376 cid/455 hp V-8**


**Condition #2 value:[$34,400](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/camaro/2020/2020-chevrolet-camaro-lt1?id=aCn1I000000kBYISA2&condition=excellent) –[$39,400](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/camaro/2021/2021-chevrolet-camaro-lt1?id=aCn1I0000008XYUSA2&condition=excellent)**


At least for now, there is no new Camaro sitting in Chevy showrooms. Until the next version goes on sale in 2029, the sixth gen (2016–24) is as fresh as it gets, and it’s largely a good value in terms of speed per dollar. Most higher-spec versions are still new enough that it will cost over $40K to get into an excellent-condition example, but early versions of the mid-range LT1 model, introduced in 2020, slid in under budget.


Available as a coupe or convertible and with either a six-speed manual or 10-speed automatic, the LT1 came with the same 6.2-liter, 455-hp V-8 as the[Camaro SS](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=2020+Chevrolet+Camaro+ss) but with lower-spec brakes, suspension, and luxury features. The LT1 was available right up through the sixth-gen Camaro’s demise after 2024, but only the 2020 and ’21 models come in under $40K in our price guide.


## 2005–10 Chrysler 300C SRT8


Stellantis


**Engine: 370 cid/425 hp V-8**


**Condition #2 value:[$23,700](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chrysler/300c/2009/2009-chrysler-300c-srt8?id=aCn1I000000DVuRSAW&condition=excellent)**


Born in the DaimlerChrysler era (1998–2007), the 300C SRT8 combined a high-horsepower Hemi with muscular sedan styling and some Mercedes-Benz suspension bits. It could scoot to 60 in 4.7 seconds and hit the quarter-mile in a little over 13 seconds—solid numbers even 20 years later. According to *Car and Driver* : “What makes the SRT8 version of Chrysler’s 300C exceptional is that it’s the first sedan from anyone, anywhere, to combine the refinement and performance of the pricey super sedans with a sticker of $42,095, no incentives necessary.”


Today, an excellent-condition early SRT8, if you can find one, can be had for barely half that sticker price, and that’s before accounting for inflation. Values have been steady and don’t show any signs of major change, so they’ll likely be a bargain for quite some time.


## 2005–07 Chevrolet Corvette (Base)


Hagerty Marketplace/GeraldRosenquist_3xqt


**Engine: 364 cid/400 hp** **V-8**


**Condition #2 value:[$35,600](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/2007/2007-chevrolet-corvette-base?id=aCn1I000000DKiYSAW&condition=excellent) –[$37,400](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/2007/2007-chevrolet-corvette-base?id=aCn1I000000DWEnSAO&condition=excellent)**


It wouldn’t be a group of high-horsepower cars at lowball prices without a Corvette in the mix, and the C6 (2005–13) is currently one of the best performance values out there. Early base models came with an LS2 V-8 rated at an even 400 hp/400 lb-ft, and in either coupe or convertible form they come in under $40K. Starting in 2008, base Corvettes upgraded to the 430-horse LS3 engine, and though LS3-powered coupes come in at $38,900 in #2 condition, convertibles squeak past the $40K mark.


## 2006–10 Jeep Grand Cherokee SRT-8


Hagerty Media


**Engine: 370 cid/420 hp** **V-8**


**Condition #2 value:[$34,200](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/jeep/grand_cherokee/2009/2009-jeep-grand_cherokee-srt~8?id=aCn1I000000DM4DSAW)**


The first Jeep product to get the SRT treatment, the original Grand Cherokee SRT-8 turns 20 this year. Back in 2006, an SUV with the heart of a muscle car was a fairly novel concept, and the SRT-8 was both quicker to 60 mph than a[Porsche Cayman S](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/cayman/2006/2006-porsche-cayman-s?id=aCn1I000000Cx2gSAC) and half the price of a Cayenne Turbo. In addition to 420 hp and 420 lb-ft from the 6.1-liter Hemi (up from 5.7 in the standard Grand Cherokee at the time), the ‘roided-up off-roader also got fat tires and a lowered ride height.


Like several of the other vehicles in this group, the Grand Cherokee SRT-8 cost Bush-era buyers around $40K from the showroom, and they are still trading for less than that today. It’s a tempting value, which is why we put the super-Jeep on our[2021 Bull Market](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/bull-market-2021/) list, but our crystal ball was a little hazy on that pick, and the #2 value has only increased a couple grand in the half-decade since.
